html:
A gold coin of the Persian Empire, introduced by Darius the Great around 515 BCE. Together with a silver coin, the siglos, it gave the empire a single money.

Persia had taken over coinage when Cyrus conquered Lydia, where the first coins had been struck, and at first it used Lydian types. The daric was very pure gold, about 8.4 grams. It showed the Great King as a running archer with bow and spear, which is why Greeks nicknamed the coins "archers".

Darics were used most in the western provinces and in dealing with Greeks. Persian gold paid for fleets and bought influence in Greek politics; during the Peloponnesian War it helped Sparta build the fleet that beat Athens. The Spartan king Agesilaus is said to have joked that he was driven out of Asia by the king's archers, meaning the bribes paid to his enemies at home. Darics went out of use after Alexander the Great conquered the empire.
sum: A gold coin of the Persian Empire, introduced by Darius the Great around 515 BCE. Together with a silver coin, the siglos, it gave the empire a single money.
